title: Russian Strikes Pummel Lakshmi Mittal's Ukrainian Steel Empire as Industry Faces Collapse
excerpt: ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine's largest steelmaker owned by Indian-origin billionaire Lakshmi Mittal, has shed thousands of jobs and shuttered units as Russian attacks, soaring energy costs, and new EU trade barriers threaten to break the country's once-formidable steel sector.
body:
• ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine's largest steel plant owned by Indian-origin billionaire Lakshmi Mittal, has closed multiple production units in 2026 and cut over 3,400 jobs amid Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.
  • The plant, located just 70 km from the front line, has seen its workforce drop from 26,000 before the war to roughly 12,000, with 2,600 employees having joined the fight and over 100 killed.
  • Russian ballistic missiles struck Ukraine's Zaporizhstal steel plant on August 11, killing seven workers — part of an escalating campaign targeting the country's industrial base.
  • New EU steel import quotas represent a 60% reduction from 2025 trade volumes, adding another existential threat to Ukraine's remaining steel producers.

The war in Ukraine is steadily dismantling the steel empire that Indian-origin billionaire Lakshmi Mittal built in the country over two decades. ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine's largest steelmaker and a subsidiary of the world's second-largest steel producer, has been forced into a cascade of closures, layoffs, and operational restrictions as Russian strikes, energy shortages, and EU regulations converge into what industry leaders describe as a fight for survival.

A Plant Under Siege

Located in southeastern Ukraine approximately 70 km from the front line, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih sits in a city that has become a frequent target of Russian missile and drone attacks. Kryvyi Rih — the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy — has been hit repeatedly, with strikes killing civilians and damaging both homes and industrial infrastructure.

https://x.com/CNNnews18/status/2089206829914227002

Before the full-scale Russian invasion in February 2022, the plant employed 26,000 workers. That number has dropped to roughly 12,000, with 2,600 employees having joined the Ukrainian armed forces and over 100 of them killed in combat.

"War dictates its own terms. We are afraid."

— Vladyslav Tyurin, senior foreman at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih

In 2026 alone, the company has announced the closure of its blooming mill, its Casting and Mechanical Plant — one of Ukraine's largest industrial enterprises — and two additional rolling mills. The cumulative job losses may reach 3,400, the company said, citing the "extremely high cost of electricity in Ukraine" and the financial unviability of operations under wartime conditions.

The August Escalation

The broader threat to Ukraine's steel sector was underscored on August 11 when Russian ballistic missiles — which Kyiv said included North Korean-supplied munitions — struck the Zaporizhstal metallurgical plant in Zaporizhzhia, killing seven workers. Russia's Defence Ministry said it targeted the Metinvest-owned facility because it produced flat-rolled steel used for military fortifications, vehicle armour, and body armour plates.

"The ballistic missile strike hit as employees were making their way to a shelter immediately after the air-raid alert was sounded," parent company Metinvest Group said. The attack brought production to a complete halt.

Russian strikes have also hit energy substations and power plants across the country, forcing rolling blackouts that have crippled energy-intensive industries like steelmaking. ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih has told staff to stay home or work remotely during periods of heightened threat.

EU Trade Barriers Add Pressure

As if Russian attacks were not enough, Ukraine's steel producers now face a new obstacle from their own allies. The European Union's introduction of the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) from January 2026, without exceptions or transition periods for Ukrainian producers, has effectively closed the European market to a significant portion of Ukrainian metallurgical products.

New EU steel import quotas, announced in August, represent a 60% reduction from 2025 trade volumes, according to Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center. Ukraine's Federation of Employers warned the restrictions could cost the country $1.2 billion in foreign earnings and reduce GDP by 0.6%.

An Indian Billionaire's Costly Stake

For Lakshmi Mittal, one of the world's wealthiest people of Indian origin, the Ukrainian investment has become a costly test of commitment. ArcelorMittal acquired the Kryvyi Rih steelworks in 2005 as part of its global expansion. Before the war, the plant exported 85% of its finished products, mainly to the Middle East and Africa. Those routes have been disrupted by attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea corridor, forcing a shift toward European markets — now themselves restricted by CBAM and quotas.

The company has highlighted its humanitarian aid in Ukraine and its efforts to support staff, but the financial toll continues to mount. A 30% increase in domestic freight tariffs this month, intended to cover the state railway's war-inflated costs, has added yet another burden.

"For us to survive until the end of the year, a lot of different things need to happen," said Oleksandr Kalenkov, president of industry association Ukrmetallurgprom, describing the situation facing Ukraine's entire steel sector.
nri_angle: Lakshmi Mittal, one of the most prominent Indian-origin business leaders globally and chairman of the world's second-largest steel producer, faces mounting losses from the war that highlight how geopolitical conflict can impact diaspora-led multinational enterprises.
